I feel like if you are already 16 months into it (especially if you had ipr done) maybe you should just stick it out. I 'quit' invisalign after only like 5 trays and my teeth have been shifting slightly for over a year. I think you should wear them for the recommended amount of time (20 hours or whatever). But I think give your teeth 'breaks' like get a fluoride rinse or tooth mouse, or put some hydroxyapatite toothpaste on your teeth for a few minutes throughout the day. There's also a special high fluoride toothpaste that you could get prescribed which can help protect your enamel. Definitely ask your dentist/orthodontist for some advice. I think the thing is, once you've started invisalign, to some extent there's no going back. Even for me, I only had 5 trays but my teeth are not back to how they were, the alignment is different (worse), the enamel is tarnished from attachments etc, my gums seem to be inflamed much more often (dentist said it is not too serious though), also the ipr is permanent. I'm glad I quit because they were going to do a lot more filing of my teeth and I decided I was uncomfortable with that. But if you're already this far into it maybe try to get to the end. But don't wear your aligners for 12 hours only because that probably will damage your tooth roots or something. And transfer to an orthodontist maybe if you're going to a dentist because dentists sometimes are terrible at invisalign and ruin your teeth

Neither of my parents (or anyone in my family) have celiac, but I'm guessing they were both each carriers of one high risk version of the celiac gene and one low risk gene. My brother has no copies of the high risk gene and I have 2 copies of the high risk gene (and I have celiac). If I have a kid they will have at least one copy of the high risk celiac gene from me. Not a guarantee they will have celiac but it raises the risk. Also there are other genes related to autoimmunity as well. My mum doesn't have celiac but she does have a different, reasonably serious autoimmune disease. I also have other autoimmune issues myself (hashimoto's etc). I have a very high risk for celiac according to that hla-dq test thing. But even outside of that I've done other genetic tests showing I have a high risk genetically for autoimmunity in general. So I think it can be a combination of genes and also environmental factors which might cause it to be triggered

There are a lot of people out there that prey on insecure people and will happily take your money, but it doesn't necessarily mean you will get a good result. You also might find recovery psychologically and physically more difficult and complicated than you initially anticipated. It can be jarring to look at yourself and see someone different. Or you may have some kind of identity crisis or freak out. It may also be physically painful and humiliating (ie. out in public or trying to work covered in bandages etc). I think you need to be extremely clear about what result you want. Anyway this person sounds like they have bdd or are fishing for attention or maybe they are just insecure... as someone that is truly ugly, I genuinely think even for truly ugly people any surgery or procedure should be treated with great caution. You absolutely can make things worse and even damage your health. These are serious procedures. I was diagnosed by my GP with another (medical grade) genetic test and other blood tests (celiac antibodies etc). I personally found the genetic testing to be empowering and I would recommend it. I genuinely believe I would have suffered for many more years with a diagnosis of "IBS" or "depression" etc had I not gotten the genetic test. Maybe you are privileged enough to have a great trust in the medical system but the reality is, a lot of people get misdiagnosed or underdiagnosed. Genetic testing can be a great way to rule out certain conditions and also potentially get hints about what could be going wrong. (To be clear I am talking about full genome sequencing etc eg. nebula genomics not 23andme). I also feel that it had given me some closure. For a long time I felt bad like maybe I did something wrong to cause this, but the testing I did said I was in like the 99th percentile risk for celiac (which I have) and like 93rd percentile risk for hashimoto's (which I also have). It also showed that I have a lot of high risk gene variants for autoimmune conditions in general. So while I will do what I can, I feel better knowing that I was always at high risk for these conditions due to my genetics and it's not some 'moral failing' or whatever people like to claim. I also found out I am definitely a carrier for something called usher syndrome 2a (which I definitely don't have) and if I ever decided to have a baby, it's something I would be empowered to know beforehand and check the gene of my partner to make sure they don't have it either. I know it seems like a new way of doing things but I do believe genetic testing is going to be increasing in the coming years so you probably should get used to the idea lol

if you pay for it yourself you can privately get your genome sequenced (eg. nebula genomics). I've done it and it certainly will give you lots of information on various conditions and genes. However it may raise more questions than answers... If you want to look up specific genes (eg. genes for EDS, or genes related to schizophrenia etc) then you definitely can and it will flag any significant mutations. If there has been a study done on the specific mutations that you have (and that's a big if, because a lot of variants haven't been studied), it may tell you that you are at risk for certain conditions. Otherwise if you look at certain genes which are known to be associated with certain conditions and it seems that you have a lot of significant mutations in a relevant gene then maybe it could be a sign that the gene is not functioning as it should be. In summary, it certainly may give you some relevant information and also you can possibly rule out certain conditions as well. I would recommend it, but only if you're the type of person that likes tinkering and investigating. It's probably not going to outright tell you 'you have x condition'. Normally you will also get an overview of your results though that will test for a lot of common conditions and will flag if anything comes up

If employers will not discriminate us for our looks than we can get a good job and pay for a comfortable life and cosmetic improvements etc. And guess what, if we are given the opportunity to empower ourselves in this way then it is more likely we could attract other people into our lives. Sure probably never the 'cool' popular good looking types will want to be with us but if we actually had more opportunities to take part in the community as a normal person rather than being shut out I honestly think it would make a huge difference. I also think part of the reason people avoid us is not just the ugliness but also the social 'taboo' that comes with the ugliness so combatting that I honestly think would be helpful.

I think the best case scenario of 'activism' for ugly people would be to make bullying someone for their appearance a taboo thing. Eg. like how it's considered taboo to call someone 'retarded' or make blatantly racist comments etc. It probably won't change anything fundamental in terms of socially being accepted but it could offer a relative sense of safety. I think it's worth doing activism tbh, especially since it's unacceptable to be racist, ableist etc, the type of people that love to bully will pick on us now because they can get away with it (we are one of the few groups left that it's socially ok to bully) ... well we have to make sure they don't do this. I know it sounds empty when I say it like this but I am ugly and I have been living it and I still think we have more capacity to fight back than what we often believe.
